accuracy.evidence: Follows Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008, Psychological Science in the Public Interest): the meshing hypothesis needs a crossover interaction where style-matched groups beat mismatched ones, and almost no studies met that design or supported it. The lab and adult text say the scores are a toy model following the direction of the research, and dual coding and retrieval practice are presented as better-supported strategies (Mayer; Roediger and Karpicke 2006).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets three beliefs common among children and teachers: that a style label limits what you can learn from (challenge 'She can only learn from pictures', m5 Lena skipping reading), that matched lessons raise scores (step 2 prediction 'Each group does best in its own style', m4 Tom), and that preferences are fake (m8 and challenge 'No, likes are made up'), separating a real like from a learning advantage.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmyth is the only lab that runs a crossover experiment: two style groups each taught a map with a picture and with words, shown as four score bars so the missing interaction is visible. It then matches topics (map, French sound, knot) to modes and compares study plans a week later. flagdelib, flagidea, flagsketch and the memory labs model practice, ideas and drawing, and the 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child first meets Mia, Leo and Ava and sees that likes are real, then runs the test and sees both 'picture' and 'listening' kids score 7 with the picture and 4 with words, so the claim fails in front of them. The topic step makes the content-decides rule concrete, and the last two steps show words plus pictures (4 versus 7) and self-testing (6 versus 3) helping everyone.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions carry the tempting myth answer: 'What will the test show?' (Each group does best in its own style), 'Which lesson will people remember more of?' (Both the same) and 'Which plan helps most a week later?' (Study in your style or Re-read 3 times). Each is tested by the bars straight after, with 'You predicted ... spot on' or a correction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with shuffled answers and ten m= messages tied to the wrong pick, for example 'No careful test found that. When lessons matched styles, scores stayed the same.' and 'Re-reading feels easy but fades fast. Testing yourself makes memories last.' A summary card stays on the canvas and feedback is read out through an aria-live status line.

readability.evidence: Kid text is four paragraphs pitched for ages 10 to 11, with the terms visual, listening and doing learners explained in everyday words and concrete topics (a map, a French word, a knot); it passed the validator's band limit. The adult side names the meshing hypothesis, the VAK label, EEF metacognition and dual coding, and the common mistake of treating a preference as an ability.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph carries one idea: the claim, the test that failed it, the topic decides, and what helps everyone. The adult side gives the evidence, the common mistake, the curriculum link and what the lab does. The family tip is a specific five-fact diagram-and-cover test, and the content gate's filler patterns all passed.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark themes show the three learners, the four crossover bars with labels and 'of 10' scores, and the study-plan bars fully on the canvas. Bars use flat theme colours (cyan, orange, violet, green) with theme text labels beside them, buttons wrap in the control row, and the walk gate passed every Show me on phone and desktop.

accessibility.evidence: axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) ran clean in both themes on desktop and phone. The canvas aria-label updates with every result (e.g. 'Words and pictures: 7 of 10 facts remembered.'), every canvas tap has a labelled button ('Meet Mia', 'Run the test'), and Challenge answers are real buttons in a labelled group with aria-live feedback.
